paragraphs.text: A Finite-Resource Network Defense Decision Method Based on a Nonzero-Sum Differential Game

runs.text: A Finite-Resource Network Defense Decision Method Based on a Nonzero-Sum Differential Game

paragraphs.text: Abstract—To address cross-asset attack propagation and limited defense capacity in multi-asset networks, this paper establishes a complete-information, nonzero-sum, open-loop differential game. The network state is described by the compromised fraction of each asset to characterize how a defender dynamically deploys defensive resources. Continuous-time strategies are parameterized using piecewise-constant controls. By combining fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration, sequential least-squares programming, and alternating best responses, a dynamic defense action decision algorithm (ABR-DAD) is developed to calculate isolation and recovery intensities for each asset and time interval. A directed multi-asset propagation network is constructed to examine the spatiotemporal allocation of resources under different defense capacities. Dynamic defense, fixed-mean defense, and no defense are compared in terms of compromised states and cumulative losses under the same time-varying attack sequence. Simulations show that the computed plans satisfy per-time capacity constraints and yield differentiated resource allocation. Dynamic defense achieves lower cumulative weighted compromise loss and cumulative comprehensive defense loss than both reference schemes, demonstrating the effectiveness of the method for calculating dynamic defensive actions under finite resources.

paragraphs.text: Introduction

A multi-asset network comprises interrelated logical assets, including entry services, business processing, identity authentication, and core data. Attacks can propagate from entry points to downstream assets along directed paths, causing compromise across multiple assets and business losses. A defender can suppress outgoing propagation through source-side isolation or reduce local compromise through recovery. These actions differ in security effects, business impacts, and resource consumption. Under limited capacity, the defender must account for the attacker’s strategy when determining the type, intensity, and timing of defensive actions.

paragraphs.text: Regarding network propagation control and resource allocation, Preciado et al.[1] studied the allocation of protection resources to inhibit spreading processes in directed networks. Al-Eiadeh and Abdallah[2] allocated defense resources to interdependent systems using attack graphs and PageRank. Paarporn and Xu[3] examined resource tradeoffs between preventive and reactive defenses, while Chen et al.[4] investigated the effects of protection and recovery investments and node priorities on network robustness. These studies provide a basis for characterizing propagation structure, asset importance, and defense costs.

paragraphs.text: In network attack–defense games, Shao and Li[5] used a multistage attack–defense graph to examine resource allocation during sequential attacks. Hu et al.[6] optimized moving-target defense through a Markov differential game, and Lou et al.[7] studied dynamic collaborative defense in crowdsensing networks under incomplete information. Huang and Zhu[8] used a susceptible–infected–susceptible (SIS) propagation model and a differential-game framework to study virus suppression and adaptive adjustment of connection weights in complex networks. Mi et al.[9] introduced stochastic disturbances into network attack–defense state evolution and developed a stochastic differential-game model for defense strategy selection. Tian et al.[10] studied a nonzero-sum attack–defense game for malware propagation in cloud environments. Zhang et al. investigated real-time defense in scale-free networks[11] and potential differential-game decisions in complex networks[12]. Sun et al.[13] incorporated action and timing choices into a time differential game. These works provide methodological foundations for analyzing strategic interactions alongside network-state evolution.

paragraphs.text: Game Model

A complete-information, two-player, noncooperative, nonzero-sum, open-loop differential game is defined on the continuous-time state system. At the planning origin, both players know the network topology, initial state, model parameters, objective functions, and constraints, and separately choose open-loop control plans over the horizon.

paragraphs.text: ABR-DAD Defense Action Computation

Based on the best-response principle for dynamic noncooperative games[17] and related iterative work[22], we design Alternating Best Response for Dynamic Defense Action Decision (ABR-DAD). Its purpose is to produce a defense action plan: holding the attack plan fixed, optimize isolation and recovery; then, holding the defense plan fixed, compute the attack response; and alternate until the numerical stopping conditions are met. The procedure is shown in Algorithm 1.

paragraphs.text: Defense Resource Allocation

The experiment first reports the defender’s resource inputs and concrete actions across control intervals to assess spatiotemporal computability and capacity feasibility. Under BD=1.2, G uses capacities 0.843705, 1.200000, 1.200000, 1.200000, 1.065570, and 0.337751 in the six intervals. The capacity bound is active in intervals 2–4 and slack in the others. With BD=0.6, capacity is fully used in the first five intervals; with BD=1.8, all intervals retain slack, as shown in Figure 2. Input decreases in the last interval under all three capacities, reflecting the tradeoff between finite-horizon protection benefits and action costs. Accordingly, the defender allocates capacity in view of state evolution and action costs rather than applying fixed-proportion static allocation; the plan exhibits both capacity saturation and investment contraction.

paragraphs.text: Conclusion

This paper establishes a nonzero-sum, open-loop differential-game model that incorporates rational attack choices and cross-asset propagation, and proposes ABR-DAD for dynamic defense action decision-making. Simulations show that the algorithm produces differentiated allocations across time intervals and assets under all three defense capacities. Under the same attack sequence, dynamic defense reduces cumulative comprehensive defense loss relative to both no defense and fixed-mean defense, and mitigates compromise accumulation at entry and key internal assets during most intervals. Late crossovers in certain asset states further indicate the need to evaluate defense plans using a comprehensive objective encompassing time-accumulated compromise and action costs. Future work will calibrate propagation rates and defense costs using measured security-operation data and extend network scale and execution feedback to assess defense-plan updates under real operational conditions.

rows: Algorithm 1. Alternating Best Response for Dynamic Defense Action Decision (ABR-DAD)Input: G, x0, T, K, B_D, B_A, parameters theta, stopping tolerances epsilon, iteration limit M.Output: defense actions D, resource use R, final controls, J_D, diagnostic results.1  Initialize feasible z_D^(0), z_A^(0).2  for m = 0, 1, ..., M-1 do3    Fix z_A^(m); use RK4 and SLSQP to compute local defender response z_D^(m+1).4    Fix z_D^(m+1); use RK4 and SLSQP to compute local attacker response z_A^(m+1).5    Test single-start unilateral deviations; compute gap_D and gap_A.6    Compute stationarity residual stat, response distance dist, capacity violation viol.7    if both SLSQP runs exit normally and three stopping metrics pass: break.8  end for9  Run three-start deviation checks and integration refinement; compute trajectories, D_i,k and R_i,k.10 Return D, R, final plans, J_D, diagnostics.
